title: The architects who built their own tools
subtitle: Why the fee fight is the wrong fight, why software lock-in is quietly eating practice margins, and seven tools that help practices earn better fees by working differently.
author: Allister Lewis
html:
This week's partner: Cogram - Give your team back the hours lost to project admin

Most architects didn’t spend years training to write up meeting notes and dig through email chains, yet that is where a large part of the week goes. Cogram is an AI platform built for architects and engineers that takes this work off the team’s plate. It produces meeting minutes in your own templates, files and searches project correspondence, turns dictated site observations and photos into field reports, and logs RFIs and submittals. It works alongside the tools you already use, including Teams, Outlook, Zoom and Autodesk, and it is SOC 2 Type II certified with no AI models trained on your data.

Image

Book a demo and mention it was ADDD who referred you.

Hi there,

Both of my posts this week deal with the same question from opposite ends, which is how much of its own economics an architecture practice actually controls. The first looks at money going out, in the form of software licences tied to a handful of vendors who set both the price and the direction of travel. The second looks at value coming in, and argues that the route to better fees runs through how we work rather than how loudly we ask for more. In both cases the practices that are doing well are the ones that have stopped waiting for someone else to fix the problem for them.

Below you'll find both posts, a live session on real-time digital twins, three events worth your time before Christmas, six new tools in the ADDD Database, and a product role at a company using AI to check drawings for compliance.

Let's get into it. 👇

What Sparked the Most Discussion This Week

Architects don't have a fee problem. They have a productivity problem.

Image
See full post here

Software cost is becoming structurally unsustainable. Not because of too many tools, but because of a dependency on a few.

Image
See full post here

Featured Live session

From Data to Decisions: Real-Time Digital Twins in Practice

Monday 16 November, 18:00 to 19:00 GMT, online. Register here

Every architect has had a client approve the drawings, then see the finished building and say it isn't what they pictured.

Real-time digital twins are one of the ways the industry is closing that gap. In plain terms, a digital twin is a live 3D version of a building or place, often built from the same Revit or Rhino model you already have, which clients, planners and communities can explore and use to make decisions before anything is fixed.

That idea ran through From Data to Decisions, the white paper I wrote with Epic Games, and on Wednesday 4 November I am taking it further in a live session with people who build these environments for a living. Each speaker will show one project and explain what decision it supported, who made it and what would have happened without it.

Image

Who is speaking

-/ David Munro, Cityscape Digital - whose work includes the interactive planning platform for British Land's Canada Water regeneration.

-/ Dorian Vee, Imerza - who makes the case that a twin should be treated as a living asset that informs investment decisions, rather than a one-off deliverable.

-/ Sarah Causey, Implexus Lab - whose operational twin at Argonne National Laboratory moved engineers from 2D dashboards to live sensor readings in 3D and VR.

What we will get into

After the project snapshots we will move on to the questions that usually decide whether a twin succeeds or quietly stops being used:

-/ Where the data actually lives, and how many platforms it passes through on the way to the twin.

-/ Who keeps the model current after handover, when the design team has moved on.

-/ Who pays for it, and how the value is proven to the people signing off the budget.

The session is built for practice leaders and digital leads who are being asked whether twins are worth the investment and would rather hear the answer from people who have delivered them. If there is a question you would like the speakers to answer, reply to this email and I will take the strongest ones into the session.

Register here

6 new tools, from AI-native design to energy modelling in the browser

Calq - A browser-based BIM modeller where you and Calq AI build a single model together, then produce plans, sections, elevations and sheets with IFC export. The full modeller is free with an account. calq.live

Image

Interviews You Need to Watch

One Role Worth Noticing This Week

Role: Senior Product Owner - Freeda

Freeda builds an AI-assisted compliance review platform for construction, where AI reads architectural plans and flags potential non-compliances and technical experts then validate and complete those findings. This role owns the internal platform those reviewers use every day, working out which steps the AI pipeline can take over and turning reviewer feedback into shipped features. As the listing puts it, "Our reviewers are not short of opinions about what costs them time."

→ View role: Here

See all roles here: www.aectechjobs.com/search

Image

What this issue means for practice leaders

My reading of this week is that most practices are trying to fix their economics from the outside, by asking clients to pay more and by absorbing whatever their software vendors decide to charge next year. Both posts point the other way. When two or three platforms sit at the centre of your workflow, the cost and direction of your tools are set by someone else, and when the case for higher fees rests on frustration rather than better outcomes, the client sets the price.

The tools in this issue show what the alternative looks like in practice: Calq and Pinocchio-EP run in a browser and work with open formats, Ondera and SpaceSync let clients and reviewers in without a paid seat, and the Freeda role exists because someone took the time to understand exactly where reviewers lose their time.

The practical step is to find out where your own time and money actually go before you buy anything else. List the vendors at the centre of your workflow, what you pay each of them, and which single workflow you could move off one of them in the next six months. Then pick one recurring task that eats your team's week, whether that is minutes, reports or document sorting, and test one of the tools above against it. If you would like help doing that properly, my practice technology workshop is designed for exactly this, or you can book a 30-minute call to talk it through.

If you would like help making these decisions across the whole practice, that is what the ADDD workshop is for: a half-day session, in person or online, that looks at where technology creates friction across your workflows and ends with a written report on the problems, the priorities and the next steps. The easiest way to start is a 30-minute call.

That's it for this week.

Thanks for reading!

7 AI rendering tools worth paying for, sorted by how you work

I track 32 AI rendering tools, and most of them make the same promise in different packaging. These are the seven I think are worth the money, grouped by where your design lives. Digital twins point at the decision that matters most, which is the one the client makes, and they are only worth the investment when they help someone make that decision earlier and with more confidence. In each case the tool matters less than whether the decision about it is made deliberately, based on how your practice actually works.

title: Your client can now check your drawings with AI. Have you checked them first?
subtitle: AI can now check drawings against the specification and the codes, and your clients can use it too. Why you should check first, what I saw at RELEASE [AEC], and a live digital twins session on 4 November.
author: Allister Lewis
html:
This week’s partner: IMSCAD Services

IMSCAD Services have been focused on the deployment of graphical applications running in virtual environments, in this time we have evolved to become NVIDIA specialists focusing on vGPU desktop deployments and Enterprise AI projects.​

“We’ve launched a globally available WaaS (workstation as a service) platform powered by Lenovo. This provides clients the opportunity to rent high powered workstations on a per user per month or per user per week basis. This solution can handle the most challenging of graphical applications, HPC workloads and AI Projects.”

Image

We offer full pre-sales consultation and professional services to assist with scoping these solutions.

https://www.imscadservices.com Email [email protected]

Hi there,

AI tools can now check a set of drawings against the specification, the schedules and the codes far faster than a person can, and nothing stops a client or a contractor from running those checks on the information you send them. Structured AI already does this, and it will not be the last. That changes the question for practices. It is no longer whether you can justify checking your own work this way, but whether you are comfortable with someone else finding the problems first.

The catch is that these checks are only as good as the information underneath them. At the Symetri Technology User Day, nearly two thirds of the room named AI as the biggest pressure on their practice, yet only six of the 28 people who answered would describe their own data as good, and AI reads whichever version it finds and answers with complete confidence.

Frank Nagle's piece in Harvard Business Review suggests part of the answer, because compliance is quickly becoming shared ground that practices cannot compete on, so the standards behind it are worth building together rather than alone. Real-time digital twins push the same question further, since a twin is only useful if the information behind it is trusted and kept up to date, and that is what we will be discussing in a live session with Epic Games on Monday 16th November.

title: Compliance software in AEC: 19 tools, 4 categories
subtitle: My AEC Magazine piece is out. Nineteen compliance tools across four categories, what actually separates them, and the question that decides which one fits your practice.
author: Allister Lewis
html:
Hi there,

A few weeks ago I posted a list of the compliance tools I could name. Martyn Day at AEC Magazine saw it and asked whether it would make an article. It is now in the September/October issue, and this week's newsletter is given over to it.

The short version is that two years ago there were a handful of these tools and there are now nineteen. That growth is not an accident. Rule-based checking has existed in AEC for years but it needed someone to translate written regulation into machine readable rules and then keep maintaining them. AI models can read the regulation as it is actually written, which removes that step. That is the reason compliance has become one of the fastest growing categories in the database.

Below: the full landscape, the distinction that decides which tool is any use to you, and what changes when your client is running the same checks on your package.

Let's get into it. 👇

Compliance software in AEC

Two years ago there were a handful of compliance tools helping AEC professionals navigate building codes and regulations. There are now at least nineteen.

Image

The piece runs across three pages in the September/October issue and covers four things: what compliance actually means on a project, the nineteen tools and how they group, who is doing the checking now that these tools are not aimed only at architects, and what happens when one of them misses something.

The part I would point you to first is the definition. Compliance on a project is doing at least four separate jobs - statutory Building Regulations, contractual Employer's Requirements, the client brief, and a practice's own internal standards. All four arrive as documents and all four get called compliance, but only the first is enforced in law. A tool that is excellent at one of them tells you nothing about how it handles the others.

Read the full article at AEC Magazine

Nineteen tools, four categories

I have sorted these by what they consume, because that is also an ordering by what your practice needs to have in place before any of them are useful. All nineteen are in the ADDD Database.

1. Inside the BIM authoring tool

Requires a BIM authored model of high enough quality to interrogate. Click on the image to go to the company’s website.

AI-BOB - continuous verification against live models, covering area compliance, accessibility and BIM execution plan checks.

Image


Kestrel Labs - checks natively in Revit, tying results to the model element and citing the code section.

Image


Pirros - quality management review on the Revit project that is already open, with findings surfaced back in the model.

Image


Baumind - reads regulations, checks 3D geometry and auto-generates corrections.

Image


Archie - Revit, Archicad and BIM 360, holding meetings, notes, regulations and design changes on one timeline with code checks alongside.

Image


2. Drawing sets and PDFs

No BIM required, which suits an industry that still demands PDF deliverables.

Helonic - works from 2D PDFs across cross-sheet consistency, code, schedules, references and specs in a single pass.

Image


MarkedUp - sheet index audits, callout verification and schedule sync, positioned as a final audit rather than a first pass.

Image


Archiboost - code compliance and QA/QC with a firm knowledge hub that draws on past project detailing.

Image


Freeda - AI plus expert human review, returning a report in hours

Image

Uptocode - drawing, model and PDF review alongside documentation and specification intelligence, extending into code research.

Image


Tektome - reviews a whole package against statute, the client brief and a practice's own standards, showing each risk with a citation.

Image


Structured AI - QA/QC for drawing packages across both PDF drawings and native Revit models.

Image


Buildcheck - drawing review aimed at reducing authority comments, RFIs and change orders before they arise.

Image


3. Documents and specifications

Aimed at the sheer volume of information a project produces.

CODiii - connects to Google Drive or SharePoint, classifies project documents automatically and runs conflict detection and gap checks.

Image


Specset - cross-references specs, drawings, RFIs and submittals as one system.

Image


Nomic - checks drawings against what it puts at more than 380 building codes, grounded in your own project documents.

Image


Ichi - submittal reviews and document checks at scale, with a persistent memory layer for jurisdiction rules and client preferences.

Image


4. Code research and reference

No project data required, so more of a pre-compliance check on the requirements. The easiest place to start.

UpCodes - searchable code platform now connecting codes directly to specifications.

Image

Struck - regulation lookup and permit checking with cited answers, across several countries including England.

Image

A few of these sit in more than one category. Structured AI works on native Revit models as well as PDFs. Uptocode covers code research alongside package review. The categories are a way of locating where a tool would sit in your own process rather than a fixed classification.

Videos You Need to Watch

What this issue means for practice leaders

The distinction that decides whether any of these tools is useful to you is between prescriptive and performance requirements. Where a requirement is prescriptive, meaning a dimension, a U-value or a specified product, it can be tested against a drawing and a computer can now do that better than ever before. Where it is a performance requirement, such as adequate means of escape for the intended occupancy, demonstrating it takes modelling, judgement and a competent person to sign it off. Every one of the nineteen is working the prescriptive side of that line. That is the easier half of the problem, and it is worth knowing before the demo rather than after.

The second thing worth sitting on with is that only a few of these were built solely for architects. A tool that can read a drawing set does not care whose drawing set it is, so a contractor can run one on your package and so can a client before signing anything off.

The checking is going to happen either way.

What is still open is whether you see the results first or last, and that reframes the decision from productivity to exposure. So the useful question is not which of the nineteen is best. It is where your own process currently has the least visibility, or where it absorbs the most time. If you do not know the answer to that, booking a call is the quickest way to find out, and I can tell you more than any demo will.

Book a call

That's it for this week.

If you are already running one of the nineteen, I would like to know which and how it went. Reply and tell me. I read every response.

Thanks for reading!

Allister

Hi there,

This week’s two posts look at the same change from opposite ends. Neil Leach’s lecture, The Death of the Architect, argues that the first part of the practice to be automated will be the wide base of graduates and juniors who do the production work. The second post looks at what that production work actually involves in a normal week. A client changes every window at 4pm on a Friday, and someone spends time finding the windows, swapping the types, updating the details, checking the drawings and reissuing them by hand. Five AI plugins for Revit can now do most of that. Put the two posts together and the question is no longer whether this work will be automated but what practices do about the people who used to learn their craft by doing it.

Below you will find both posts, the full Beyond the Hype report from the AI roundtable we co-chaired with Revizto in London, where to find me at RELEASE [AEC] in Paris next week, the late-change workflow tools in the ADDD Database, two new videos and one role worth noticing.

Let’s get into it. 👇

What Sparked the Most Discussion This Week

Neil Leach argues the architect Alberti defined in the 1450s is dying. The first thing to go is the junior base of every practice pyramid.

Image
See full post here

5 AI Revit plugins can now handle a late client change. Most practices still do it by hand.

Image
See full post here

BEYOND THE HYPE: HOW ARCHITECTURE PRACTICES ARE REALLY USING AI

In September, heads of design technology, BIM and AI from leading international architecture practices met in London to talk honestly about AI. The discussion took place at a roundtable hosted by Revizto and co-chaired by ADDD, with contractors, consultants and software leaders also taking part.

We opened with two direct questions. Which AI tool does your practice pay for, and would you renew it tomorrow at the same price? And what is the biggest mistake practices are making with AI right now? The conversation was held under the Chatham House Rule, so people spoke far more candidly than they would on a conference stage. The report draws ten themes from what was said.

Image
Download here

The ADDD Workshop: a practical starting point for AI and technology decisions

The Workshop is a focused half-day session, held in person or online with your team, that looks at where technology and AI can help your practice and where they are currently causing friction. We begin by talking through how your team actually works, from early design through to delivery, so that the conversation is grounded in your real workflows rather than in a generic view of what a practice should be doing. From there we go through practical examples of tools that are relevant to your discipline, which gives everyone a shared and realistic picture of what is available and what is worth paying attention to.

I have been running workshops for Orms, Haworth Tompkins, Levitt Bernstein, DMWR, EPR and Morris & Co.

Image

Within the session we identify the main problems holding the practice back, agree on which opportunities are worth pursuing first, and talk openly about the cost of leaving things as they are. Within a few days you receive a written report that sets out the key findings, the priorities and the recommended next steps, so the discussion turns into something you can act on and share with the wider team or the partners.

The Workshop is intended to give you strategic clarity, and it is not a technical audit of your systems. It works well as a first step for practices that know their tools and processes need attention but are not yet sure where to begin, and it can lead on to deeper work such as a early stage workflow software, Technology Blueprint or ongoing advisory support if that turns out to be useful.

Nonica - a Revit add-in whose AI Connector lets Claude read, report on and modify your Revit model, so you can ask it to find every window of the old type and swap it for the new one. The free version is read-only, and editing needs the PRO tier. (https://nonica.io)

It is priced per user per month. (https://www.imscadservices.com) Email [email protected]

One Role Worth Noticing This Week

Role: Sustainability Consultant - Circuland

Circuland is a London startup whose SaaS platform creates Digital Passports for construction products and buildings, supporting circularity, net zero, safety and transparency. The role sits between sustainability expertise and product development: collecting and validating sustainability data at product and building level, turning regulations and industry needs into product requirements, and keeping track of standards in carbon, circularity and certification.

They are looking for someone from an architecture, engineering or wider built environment background with at least two years of sustainability experience, familiarity with BREEAM, LEED or WELL, and strong Excel and data skills. The role is hybrid, with three days a week in the London office, and equity is offered alongside salary. It is a good example of the kind of job Leach expects to grow, where built environment knowledge is combined with data and product work.

→ View role: Here

See all roles here: www.aectechjobs.com/search

Image

What this issue means for practice leaders

Read together, this week’s posts describe the same shift from two sides. Neil Leach expects the base of the practice pyramid to be automated first, and the Friday late change shows exactly what that base does: it finds the elements, swaps the types, updates the details, checks the drawings and produces something the client can react to. Each of those steps now has a tool that does most of the work, and the report from the Revizto roundtable shows that the practices furthest ahead are not asking which tool is the cleverest, but which ones they would pay for again once they have tested them against a defined purpose. The growth Leach describes in the middle of his rocket is the people who can set up and run that chain, and the Circuland role is a small example of the kind of job that sits there.

The question Leach leaves open is one practice leaders cannot leave open. If juniors no longer learn by doing the production work, the practice has to decide how they will learn instead, whether that is by reviewing what the automation produces, owning a step in the chain or working alongside the people who build it.

The practical step is to take one task that happens every month, such as a late change, and map who does each step today, which steps could be automated and what the person doing that step currently learns from it. If you would like help doing that properly, that is what the ADDD workshop is for: a half-day session, in person or online, that looks at where technology creates friction across your workflows and ends with a written report on the problems, the priorities and the next steps.

That's it for this week.

title: The hardest part of a digital twin is not the software

html:
Hi there,

Most practices are not short of data. The difficulty is that it rarely reaches the person making a decision in a form they can use, at the moment they need it. That is the thread through this week's issue, first in a white paper we have published with Epic Games and then in my conversation with Angelos Chronis about climate simulation that now runs in seconds inside the design tools architects already use.

The detail from the paper that I keep coming back to is from Argonne National Laboratory, where much of the work on a live digital twin went into turning more than 5,000 model elements into 220 sensor-linked zones, each checked against engineering drawings, before any sensor data could be placed in the right location. Geometry travels well from one tool to the next, but its meaning has to be rebuilt.

Below you will find the paper, the interview, two new tools in the database, three events on 15 October (I am speaking at one of them), a short research survey and a computational design role at BeeGraphy.

Let's get into it. 👇

What Sparked the Most Discussion This Week

From Data to Decisions: our new white paper with Epic Games

The AEC industry does not have a data availability problem. It has a data usability problem. BIM models with millions of elements, simulation outputs, live sensor feeds and now AI recommendations each sit in their own tool, and very few of the people who need to act on them can see how they fit together.

Image

From Data to Decisions, written in partnership with Epic Games, looks at how teams are using Unreal Engine to close that gap, and follows three organisations doing it in practice. Implexus Lab built a live digital twin of a liquid-metal test loop at Argonne National Laboratory, showing more than a thousand sensors in spatial context. Jacobs uses its RealScene platform to train first responders in scenarios that are too rare or too dangerous to rehearse for real. Buro Happold turns masterplans into interactive environments where planners, engineers and clients can see how a district will perform before it is built.

The paper is free to download, and everyone who downloads it will hear about the upcoming webinar first.

Image

What this issue means for you

Everything in this issue comes back to the same point, which is that the value of project information depends on who can use it and when. At Argonne, the geometry moved across without much trouble but the model only became useful once someone had rebuilt what each part of it meant, zone by zone, and checked it against the drawings.

With infrared.city, the analysis itself is not new but moving it from a specialist check at the end of a stage into the design tool while the massing is still changing alters which decisions it can influence. Two new tools make the same move on a smaller scale, with Foveate putting drawings, renders and models in front of a client in one place, and Kasper putting cost and carbon information in front of the person choosing the material. In each case the gain comes from shortening the distance between the information and the decision, rather than from producing more information.

The practical step is to pick one recurring decision on a live project, such as a façade material, a massing change or a wind comfort question on a public space, and trace it back. Write down where the information behind that decision comes from, how long it takes to arrive, what has to be converted or re-entered along the way, and who actually sees it before the decision is made. Wherever meaning is being rebuilt by hand, or the answer arrives after the design has moved on, that is where a tool or a workflow change will pay back first, and where it is worth testing against the software you already pay for before buying anything new. title: The prediction I got wrong this year
subtitle: Architecture. Technology. Workflows.
author: Allister Lewis
html:
Hi there,

I'm out of the office this week, so this is a shorter one - no new tools, no roles, no posts. Normal service resumes next week.

Instead, some mid-year notes. Eight months, tens of practices interviewed, and one prediction I got properly wrong. Plus what changes here from September.

Let's get into it. 👇

Three things that changed in 2026

1. The question moved from "which tool" to "who decides".

In January I was mostly asked what to buy. Now I'm asked who should own it, who signs it off, and what happens when the person who championed it leaves. That's a more mature question and a harder one.

2. Software spend became visible.

Renewal costs have climbed far enough that directors are looking at the bottom line properly for the first time. Once you look, you nearly always find licences nobody opens and two tools doing one job.

3. Vendors started asking about practices.

The interesting shift this year is on the other side of the table. Software companies are increasingly aware they don't understand how architecture practices actually make decisions and that this, not the product, is why the sale stalls.

And one thing that didn't

The bottleneck is still organisational, not technical. The tools are ready. The practices, mostly, aren't - not because people are resistant but because nobody owns the decision, nobody has time to run a proper pilot and nothing survives contact with people who are busy ono a project.

I said this in January. I'd say it harder now.

The prediction I got wrong

I thought AI adoption would be high by now. I was wrong, and not by a small margin.

Across the interviews I've run this year with practices of all sizes, the picture is consistent: there is an enormous amount of noise, and very little of it has landed in anyone's actual workflow. People are experimenting. A few individuals are getting real value. But for most of the practices I spoke to, AI is not yet a meaningful part of how work gets done.

That gap between conversation volume and genuine use is the most interesting thing I've found all year. It means the practices moving deliberately now are not late. They're early, and they still have room to do it properly rather than in a panic.

If you're sitting there feeling behind - you're probably not.

What changes here from September

A few things I want to flag, because they change what you get from ADDD.

A weekly show reviewing five new tools.

Rather than tools appearing in the database with a one-line description, they'll be reviewed properly on camera each week. The database now sits at around 1,900 tools, and it deserves better than just a list.

An annual State of AEC Technology report.

Published each March. What practices actually run, what they pay, what they've dropped, and how you compare. The benchmark doesn't exist at the moment, which is exactly why the interviews this year have been so revealing.

Fixed prices on everything.

No more bespoke proposals for standard work. You'll be able to see what something costs before you speak to me.

The through-line is the same as always: better decisions come from better information, and there is far less independent information in this market than there should be.

I am really excited about this as it will deliver true value for architects.

Hi there,

Most of the work in architecture now is retrofit. Extensions, conversions, refurbishments, deep retrofits - existing buildings, not blank sites. And yet almost every technology stack on the market is still designed as if you're starting from nothing.

That gap is this week's throughline. I put together a 2026 stack built specifically for existing buildings - scan, layouts, spec, compliance, material reuse - and the interesting part isn't any single tool. It's that the tooling has finally caught up to where the work actually is.

Three things this week. The existing-building stack. The AI compliance landscape, which has gone from a handful of tools to fifteen-plus in two years. And a diagnostic that names the real constraint - which, for most practices, isn't the software at all.

Theme of the Week

The bottleneck moved

Three posts, one underlying shift: the technology is no longer the hard part.

Look at the retrofit stack. Two years ago, building a credible tech stack for existing buildings meant gaps everywhere - the scans was clumsy or 2D, the layouts were manual, the compliance check didn't exist. Now there's a tool for each stage, most of them affordable, most working inside or alongside Revit. The work moved to retrofit and the tooling followed.

The compliance landscape says the same thing louder. A category that had a handful of players two years ago now has fifteen-plus, segmented by where they sit in your workflow - inside the BIM model, across drawing sets, through full specification intelligence, into code research. That's not hype. That's a category maturing fast enough that the question is no longer "does a tool exist" but "which stage of my process has no visibility."

Which is exactly what the diagnostic post argues. Most practices think they're behind on AI. They're not - everyone is. The tools exist, they're proven, and they're affordable. What's broken isn't access. It's how the decisions get made: reactively, on partial advice, with no one owning the change.

So the constraint has moved. It used to be the software. Now it's the decision-making around the software. The practices that pull ahead won't have the best tools - they'll just choose better, and match what they buy to where their work actually is.

Second: I ran an experiment at home. Building a golf simulator room for my son, I deliberately avoided the default tools. Rayon for 2D layout. Qonic for 3D. Gendo for visuals. Claude for material quantities. None of it required a training course. None of it cost four figures a year. And it worked. Third: five ConTech companies raised over $55m last week. That capital goes on people. And the people it's looking for have domain knowledge - which means AEC professionals are in a better position than they might think.

Theme of the Week

A thread runs through everything this week: the gap between what UK architecture practices could engage with, and what they actually do.

At AIA 2026, architects showed up as decision-makers. They evaluated tools. They met vendors. They participated in the business of practice alongside the craft of it. The RIBA's 2026 programme - 27 pages of regional talks and branch socials - asks something different of its members. Smaller. More internal. Less connected to the commercial reality of running a practice.

That's not a criticism of any individual event. It's a structural observation about professional self-image. When a body builds an expo at this scale, it signals to its members that their role extends beyond delivering buildings - to understanding, evaluating, and adopting the tools that make practice viable. UK architects, broadly, have not been given that signal.

The lighter tool stack experiment this week is the same pattern at the individual level. Revit and SketchUp dominate by default - not because they're always the right answer, but because nobody has questioned the assumption. The experiment showed that a ramp now exists where a cliff used to be. Browser-first, sensibly priced tools can handle feasibility, early design, and small projects without the overhead of a full production environment.

The funding news closes the loop. ConTech companies raised $55m last week and are actively looking for people with domain knowledge. AEC professionals are a hiring priority. But you have to be in the room - or at least aware the room exists - to benefit from that.

The cost of opting out isn't prestige. It's knowledge, leverage, and the gap between what technology could do for your practice and what it's actually doing.

Hi there,

80% of companies are now using AI. Two years ago it was 33%.

That number came from The Guardian. What it didn't say is that most of that adoption is tactical - isolated tools, individual habits, no strategy underneath.

AI capability is doubling every four months. Your software stack isn't keeping pace. Your team structure isn't keeping pace. Your data isn't keeping pace.

And architecture practices are especially exposed - because the sector has spent a decade accumulating technology without designing it.

The gap isn't access. Every director with a laptop has access to AI. The gap is between the data that exists in your practice and the data that's actually usable by any of it.

I spent time at Digital Construction Week 2026 this week - talking to 12 ConTech companies, across two simple questions. The answers were different. The problem wasn't.

That same thread - data you can't use - ran through every conversation on the floor.

When AI capability doubles again in Q4, practices with a clear technology strategy will use that leap. Practices without one will buy another subscription and wonder why nothing changed.

But a number like that can mislead. Adoption and strategy are different things. Buying access to a tool and building the conditions for that tool to work are not the same investment.

Three posts this week circled the same underlying point from different angles.

The first made the strategic case directly - AI capability is doubling roughly every four months. The practices that will benefit from that growth aren't the ones who bought the most subscriptions. They're the ones who built something underneath them. A technology strategy. A data architecture that AI can actually read.

The second came from conversations at DCW 2026. Twelve companies. Two questions each. What struck me wasn't how different the products were - it was how consistent the problem was. Buried data. Knowledge lost at project handover. Specialists holding information that non-specialists can't access. The gap between data that exists and data that's usable.

James Bell from Symetri put it plainest: "Are you creating consistent, high quality, accurate data? Because that's what you're preparing for AI." Not AI itself. The foundation AI needs to work.

The third reframed DCW's speaker programme as a signal - not a content calendar. The investment concentrations visible in the programme (AI and automation, BIM and data management, reality capture) map directly to the roles that will open in the next 12-18 months. The practices and professionals who read that signal now are the ones who will be positioned for it.

The common thread: access to AI tools is not the bottleneck. The bottleneck is whether your data is in good enough shape to use them.

Hi there,

Ferrari revealed a car this week and the internet lost its mind. Not because the car was bad - because it was different. The Luce broke from everything Ferrari had looked like for decades and the reaction was instant: rejection dressed up as critique.

Architecture practices do the same thing with technology. A tool gets proposed, a workflow gets challenged and the room fills with concerns. Some of those concerns are valid - practices have been burned before. But some of the resistance isn't really about the tool. It's about the change itself.

Tim Bailey said it plainly: "Most of an architect's work can be systemised to a greater degree. Resistance to that is cultural."

Not technical. Not financial. Cultural. That's the conversation worth having this week.

Let's get into it. 👇

What Sparked the Most Discussion This Week

Theme of the Week

Cultural resistance is your real technology problem. Not budget. Not software selection. Not implementation complexity. The Ferrari moment - that instant rejection when something breaks from familiar form - happens in practices every week.

A new workflow gets proposed and the experienced people in the room raise concerns. The concerns feel technical. They're often cultural. And the distinction matters because they require completely different responses. Technical concerns get resolved with better information. Cultural resistance requires a structured process for working through it - not around it, not past it.

Ferrari's CEO said people are afraid of everything new. That's too broad to be useful. What's more precise: people are afraid of losing what works. In practices with hard-won processes and real institutional memory, that fear is rational. The question is whether there's a structured way to surface it, name it, and move through it.

The workflow stacks idea posted this week is connected to this. The standard software conversation - "what tool should we use?" - treats tools as isolated decisions. They're not. The same Revit licence produces different outcomes in two practices depending on what sits around it. Mapping complete stacks - how software connects, where data flows, where friction lives - is a more honest frame. It moves the conversation from tool selection to system design. That's a different room to be in.

Hi there,

NXTBLD 2026 is done. Two days on the floor, 50+ exhibitors, and one question running through everything: how do you make sense of it all?

The AEC software market isn't small anymore. It's sprawling - design tools, BIM platforms, digital twins, AI-assisted drawing, MEP automation, compliance engines, data connectors. And that's before you get to the infrastructure layer of SDKs, hardware and resellers holding it together.

The problem isn't a shortage of options. The problem is knowing which ones matter for your practice specifically.

Theme of the Week: The market is mature enough to be confusing. That's the real problem.

Three posts this week. One thread running through all of them.

At NXTBLD, the scale of the AEC software market was impossible to ignore - 50+ exhibitors across design, engineering, infrastructure, digital twins, compliance, plugins, and SDKs. The breadth is no longer a sign of immaturity. It's a sign that the market has grown faster than most practices' ability to evaluate it.

Day one left me with a clear conviction: the tools are available. The problem is the ways of working they're meant to support haven't changed in 10-15 years. Duplication. Manual workflows. Cultural resistance to change. These aren't technology problems - they're organisational ones. New software doesn't fix them on its own.

And then there's UKREiiF. While the floor at NXTBLD showed the range of what's possible, the developer conference circuit is starting to show what's expected. Technology capability is becoming a procurement signal. Practices that can articulate their AI policy, name a digital design lead, and demonstrate data security thinking are pulling ahead on longlists - not because of portfolio, not because of awards, but because developers are making fast judgements about delivery risk.

The through-line: the software explosion has outpaced adoption. And the practices that close that gap - not by buying more tools, but by embedding the right ones into a clear strategy - are the ones that will be competitive in the next five years.

When a senior architect walks out the door, they don't just leave a vacancy. They take with them decades of design intent, hard-won technical judgement, and institutional memory that no PDF, folder, or BIM file was ever designed to capture.

This is the Knowledge Cliff and according to a major new white paper from D.TO and AEC Tech Hub, the AEC industry is approaching it fast. Retirements, staff turnover, faster project timelines, and permanent distributed delivery are all accelerating the crisis. The informal mechanisms that once sustained knowledge - mentorship, proximity, long project cycles - are no longer sufficient.

❝

"Our young designers are brilliant but too often knowledge about constructability, standards, and sustainability lives in a few people's heads or buried in past projects."

Johnathan Soto, BIM Manager - ADG Blat

The consequences are tangible: repeated reinvention of details, inconsistent standards across offices, slower onboarding, and sustainability targets that erode before a building is even occupied. And crucially, the white paper argues this isn't just an operational headache - it's a governance and competitiveness issue that hits margins, client confidence, and ESG credibility directly.

WHAT’S INSIDE THE WHITE PAPER

01 The knowledge crisis in AEC

Why retirements and faster timelines are creating a cliff, not a gradual slope and what's accelerating it now.

02 The real cost of missing knowledge

How knowledge gaps drive RFIs, rework, margin erosion, and weakened sustainability performance.

03 Structural gaps holding firms back

BIM silos, unstructured data, manufacturer knowledge gaps, and the ownership vacuum when knowledge is everyone's job, it's no one's.

04 D.TO's system architecture

How governed knowledge infrastructure - with Human-Centric AI embedded into BIM workflows - addresses the problem at its root.

The white paper is backed by a real-world case study with ADG Blatt, a forward-thinking practice that used D.TO to bring constructability into the design phase, resulting in faster onboarding, fewer detailing errors, and more consistent sustainability performance across projects.

Hi there,

Why This Matters

Architecture has traditionally relied on a simple belief:

If the work is good, it will speak for itself.

That assumption is no longer holding. Visibility, opportunity, and influence in the industry are increasingly shaped by those who communicate effectively, not just those who design well.

The New Layer of Architecture: Influence

What emerged from the day is that influence is becoming a new layer of practice. Not separate from architecture, but embedded within it. It affects:

-/ who gets seen

-/ who gets trusted

-/ who gets opportunities

And increasingly, who gets work. This is not about becoming an influencer in the traditional sense. It is about recognising that communication is now a professional skill, not an optional extra.

Key Themes from the Influencer Day:

Image

1. Architecture is now part of the attention economy

We are operating in a context where attention is limited and actively competed for. Short-form video, social platforms, and rapid communication formats are reshaping how architecture is represented and understood.

Implication: The ability to communicate ideas clearly and quickly is becoming as important as the ideas themselves.

2. Good work does not travel on its own

There is a persistent gap between quality of work and visibility. Architects often assume excellence will be recognised. In practice, without communication, work remains unseen.

Implication: Visibility is not vanity. It is a mechanism for opportunity.

3. Narrative is missing in most architectural communication

Many architects document projects but do not explain them. The strongest guidance focused on storytelling through:

-/ tension
-/ protagonist
-/ change

Explaining not just what was designed, but why it matters.

Implication: Without narrative, the value of architecture is not fully understood.

4. Positioning is critical

A consistent question throughout the day was: What do you want to be known for? Random documentation does not build recognition. Clear positioning does.

Implication: Architects and practices need a defined point of view, not just a portfolio.

5. Influence is built through consistency and authenticity

The most effective creators are not necessarily the largest, but the most consistent and authentic. This is a skill developed over time, not an inherent trait.

Implication: Influence compounds. Small, consistent actions build long-term visibility.

6. Representation is changing

Social media is expanding who has a voice in architecture. It is enabling new perspectives and reducing reliance on traditional gatekeepers.

Implication: The profession is becoming more open, but also more competitive.

7. Architects need to speak beyond architects

Much architectural communication remains insular. If content can only be understood by architects, its reach and impact are limited.

Implication: Simplifying language and broadening audience is essential.

8. Content should be embedded in practice

Content creation should not sit outside practice as an additional task. It should be captured alongside the work itself.

Implication: Documentation and communication need to be integrated into workflows, not added afterwards.

9. Influence creates leverage

Influence shapes perception, authority, and access to opportunity. It can lead to:

-/ new types of work
-/ diversified revenue streams
-/ greater control over career direction

Implication: This is not just marketing. It is strategic positioning.

Image

What This Means for Architects

Architects are no longer operating in a closed professional system. The industry is becoming more visible, more connected, and more influenced by public-facing narratives. This creates both opportunity and risk. Those who engage with this shift can:

-/ shape conversations

-/ build authority

-/ access new opportunities


Those who do not risk becoming less visible, regardless of the quality of their work.

What This Means for Practices

For practices, this extends beyond individual visibility.

It directly affects:

-/ brand positioning

-/ talent attraction

-/ client perception

-/ business development

Most practices communicate at two points:

-/ project launch
-/ project completion

The opportunity is to communicate throughout the lifecycle:

-/ Process

-/ Decisions

-/ Challenges

-/ Thinking

This creates a more continuous, credible, and differentiated narrative.

Closing

Image

This is a shift I am seeing increasingly across the industry.

Not just in how projects are delivered, but in how they are communicated and understood.

As workflows evolve, communication and positioning are becoming part of how practices operate. If you are exploring how this fits within your own practice, or how to better connect your work, workflows, and narrative, I am happy to share how others are approaching this.

title: Special Edition ATN Summit: What Is Actually Changing in Architecture
subtitle: Discovering the tools, workflows, and decisions shaping modern architectural practice
author: Allister Lewis
html:
Image

The industry is not short of tools. It is short of connected workflows.

I have just returned from the ATN Summit in London, a two-day event bringing together some of the most forward-thinking architects, technologists, and founders working in the built environment today.

For those who were not in the room, this is a concise briefing on what was actually discussed, what is working in practice, and where the industry is heading next. This is not a summary of talks. It is a distillation of the underlying patterns that emerged across the event, supported by both my own notes and observations from attendees.

The focus is on three things:

-/ what leading practitioners are doing differently
-/ where technology is genuinely delivering value
-/ what this means for architecture practices today

Image

If you are reviewing how your workflows operate across projects, I am happy to share how other practices are approaching this.

Book a call here: 30 min with Allister Lewis

The Big Shift

The clearest takeaway from the ATN Summit is that the industry conversation has moved beyond tools.

Most architecture firms are still focused on tools. The leading practices are focused on workflows.

For the past decade, much of the focus has been on identifying and adopting new software. That conversation is now maturing. The leading practices are no longer asking which tools to use, but how those tools operate together across a project lifecycle.

This shift towards workflow thinking is significant. It reframes technology from a collection of isolated applications into a connected system that supports decision-making, design development, and delivery.

In practice, this is where the real gains are being realised. Not through individual tools, but through how information flows between them, how tasks are automated, and how teams operate across stages.

Image

Standout Talks and What They Mean

A number of talks stood out, not just for their content, but for what they reveal about the direction of the industry.

Aaron Perry – Qonic

Aaron Perry opened the conference with a clear articulation of the structural challenges facing the AEC industry, particularly around fragmented workflows and disconnected data. He then demonstrated how Qonic is evolving to address these issues, showing significant product development over the past nine months.

The platform has moved beyond a high-performance browser-based model viewer into an environment where users can model, manipulate geometry, and manage data within a single interface.

Implications: There is a clear move towards unified, web-based environments that reduce fragmentation across tools and workflows. This is where meaningful efficiency gains are likely to be realised.

Image

Sanne van der Burgh – MVRDV

Sanne presented MVRDV’s work through the lens of sustainability, focusing on how the practice has embedded embodied carbon tracking across its projects. A centralised dashboard enables comparison, monitoring, and informed decision-making throughout the design process.

Importantly, the presentation demonstrated that high-quality architectural design and sustainability are not competing priorities, but can be balanced within a structured system.

Implications: Sustainability is becoming a measurable and integrated part of design workflows, particularly at early stages where decisions have the greatest impact.

Gary McLuskey – Greystar

Gary McLuskey shared how Greystar is using data from tenants to inform and improve future developments. The presentation highlighted a commitment to integrated workflows, combining user data, design processes, and technology such as Giraffe to refine outcomes over time.

This reflects a developer-led approach that prioritises feedback loops and continuous improvement.

Implications: The centre of decision-making is increasingly shifting towards developers who are leveraging data to drive design outcomes. Architects need to align with this reality.

Pamela and Jesper Wallgren – Finch

Pamela and Jesper presented the evolution of Finch, from an early parametric concept into a multi-platform tool for generating and optimising layouts across Rhino, Revit, and Archicad.

Recent developments include expanded modelling capabilities and application across additional sectors such as commercial and healthcare. The decision to remain platform-agnostic is particularly notable.

Implications: Tools that integrate across existing architectural workflows, rather than replacing them, are more likely to achieve widespread adoption.

Harlan Miller – UNStudio

Harlan Miller presented a series of projects spanning several decades, illustrating the continuity between design intent and final delivery. A key example was a large-scale tower project in Dubai, where the original concept was maintained through a complex and extended delivery process.

The presentation emphasised rigour, consistency, and long-term design stewardship.

Implications: While technology is evolving, the fundamentals of architectural quality, control, and intent remain central. Workflow improvements must support, not replace, these principles.

Mollie Claypool – AUAR

Mollie Claypool presented AUAR’s approach to automated timber construction, combining digital design, robotic fabrication, and on-site manufacturing. The use of container-based robotic systems to produce building components represents a significant shift in how housing can be delivered. The ambition to scale this model, particularly in the US market, was clear.

Implications: Construction innovation is becoming increasingly integrated with design and technology. This has the potential to reshape delivery models, particularly in housing.

Across these talks, the common thread was clear. The industry is moving towards more connected, data-driven workflows where design, analysis, and delivery are increasingly integrated.

Image

10 observations from inside the room:

Image

1. The top 1% is operating differently

What was presented on stage does not reflect the industry average. It reflects what is possible when workflows are intentionally designed and consistently applied. There is a clear level of integration, control, and clarity in how leading teams operate that is not yet widespread.

What this means: A performance gap is emerging between practices that are actively designing their workflows and those that are not.

2. AI is not the main story

AI was present across the event, but it was rarely positioned as the primary focus. Most teams are still concentrating on improving delivery, coordination, and reliability. The emphasis remains on getting core processes right.

What this means: The industry is still addressing foundational workflow challenges before AI can be applied at scale.

3. Automation is where value is being realised

The most practical examples focused on automation rather than AI. This included reducing repetitive tasks, improving data flow, and connecting systems across different stages. These changes are incremental, but highly effective.

What this means: Real value is currently being delivered through operational efficiency, not speculative transformation.

4. Workflows are the real differentiator

The strongest presentations did not focus on individual tools. They demonstrated how tools operate together across a project lifecycle. This is where productivity, consistency, and quality are being improved.

What this means: Software selection alone is not enough. Competitive advantage comes from how systems are structured and used in practice.

5. BIM 2.0 is emerging, but unevenly

There is clear progress in the development of next-generation BIM tools and approaches. However, adoption and maturity vary significantly across the ecosystem. Some tools are well integrated into workflows, while others remain experimental.

What this means: Practices need to be selective and pragmatic. Not all innovation is ready to support live project delivery.

6. Sustainability is becoming embedded

Sustainability was consistently present in discussions, often linked to data, analysis, and early-stage decision-making. It is no longer treated as an isolated requirement.

What this means: Environmental performance is increasingly being addressed at the feasibility stage, where it has the greatest impact.

7. A generational shift is underway

The presence of younger architects was notable. They are more open to new tools, more collaborative in how they work, and less constrained by legacy processes. Their expectations of how practice should operate are different.

What this means: Adoption of new workflows and technologies is likely to accelerate as this group moves into more influential roles.

8. Influence is becoming part of practice

The way attendees documented, shared, and discussed the event highlighted a shift towards a more visible and connected industry. Content, communication, and audience are becoming part of professional practice.

What this means: Practices that engage with this will build stronger networks and greater visibility.

9. Events like this require real orchestration

The level of organisation, curation, and delivery was high. Bringing together this range of perspectives in a coherent way is not straightforward. It reflects a deliberate effort to create value for the community.

What this means: Curated environments like this are becoming important platforms for knowledge exchange and industry alignment.

10. The next generation will not carry legacy constraints

Many younger attendees are being exposed to advanced workflows and tools early in their careers. They are not bound by the assumptions or limitations that have shaped current practice.

What this means: Future practices will be built on different foundations, with fewer constraints and a greater emphasis on integration and efficiency.

What This Means for Architects

The consistent theme across the ATN Summit is that the industry is not constrained by a lack of tools. It is constrained by how those tools are used.

Most practices are operating with:

-/ disconnected systems across project stages
-/ unclear handovers between teams
-/ limited visibility of how information flows through a project

This creates friction, duplication, and inefficiency, particularly as projects move from early design into delivery. By contrast, the practices operating at a higher level have taken a different approach. They are not focused solely on adopting new software. They are designing how their workflows operate across the full project lifecycle, from feasibility through to construction.

Image

This includes:

-/ defining how data is created, structured, and shared
-/ integrating tools so that information flows without manual intervention
-/ automating repeatable tasks where appropriate
-/ aligning design, analysis, and delivery processes

The result is not just increased efficiency. It is better decision-making, earlier clarity, and more consistent outcomes. This is where the real opportunity now sits. Not in identifying the next tool, but in defining how practice operates as a system.

Closing

This is an area I am increasingly focused on in my work with practices:

Moving from: tool selection to workflow design

Helping teams define how their systems operate in practice, where value is created, and how technology supports better outcomes across a project lifecycle. This is the work I am increasingly focused on through workshops and advisory engagements.

If you are reviewing how your workflows operate across projects, I am happy to share how other practices are approaching this.

Most practices now have access to more technology than ever before. But very few practices have intentionally designed how those tools work together. Over time the result is a patchwork of software and processes that function independently but rarely operate as a coherent system.

Hi there,

This week’s issue sits at the intersection of three conversations that are no longer separate: AI acceleration, evolving digital roles, and the day-to-day friction inside our core tools. From Digital Construction Week to discussions around Digital Design Leadership, the signal is consistent. Architecture is not just adopting new software. It is being reshaped by workflow pressure.

What stood out most in the conversations I had this week is that many firms are experimenting at the edges, AI pilots, new plugins, reporting tools, but the structural layer beneath them remains under-designed. Infrastructure decisions, project management maturity, and performance constraints are quietly determining how much value any new tool can actually deliver.

So in this issue, I want to connect the dots. What sparked the most discussion, why Revit performance is a strategic signal rather than a technical annoyance, and what all of this means for practice leaders trying to steer through BIM 2.0 without adding more noise.

Theme of the Week: Revit Isn’t Slow. Your Infrastructure Is.

If your Revit model feels slower remotely than it did in the studio, it is rarely just “one of those things.” Over the past few years, many practices moved heavy workflows into cloud or virtual desktop environments to support hybrid working. It solved mobility but often at the cost of responsiveness. Orbiting feels heavier, syncing takes longer, regeneration lags. That friction is not random. It is systemic.

When you virtualise design software, you introduce additional abstraction layers between user and GPU, shared compute resources, and network round-trip delay. Parametric modelling tools like Revit are highly sensitive to latency. Even small delays compound into perceptible drag across a working day. This is not just an IT issue. It is a systems architecture decision affecting how quickly your teams can think, test and iterate.

Slower modelling impacts more than comfort. It affects iteration speed, morale, billable efficiency and readiness for AI-enabled workflows. If your base modelling environment is underperforming, adding more tools will not solve the problem. It will amplify it. This is where the Digital Design Leader must step in, because performance is not a technical detail. It is a workflow and business strategy choice.

No jumping between chatbots and Word. Upon sending, the platform compresses the report, tracks who has read it, issues reminders and removes the attachment chaos that slows down coordination. The result is fewer wasted hours and clearer accountability.

For practices thinking seriously about workflow performance, this is not just a note-taking tool. It is a lightweight reporting system designed for meetings, inspections and construction follow-ups. The pricing model is document-based rather than per-user, which lowers friction for teams. If your reporting process still lives in Word and email threads, this is worth a look.

Practices that treat AI as a shortcut risk hollowing out trust, creativity, and professional value. Theme of the Week: Why “Time-Saving” Software Often Increases Delivery Overhead in Architecture Practices

Many architecture practices invest in software expecting it to reduce delivery time and costs. In reality, the opposite often happens - delivery overhead increases, even when the tool technically works.

This is not a software problem. It is a workflow and decision-ownership problem.

The core misconception

Time saved by software is rarely reclaimed as fee savings.

Instead, it is usually absorbed into:

-/ additional checking and coordination

-/ parallel workflows “just in case”

-/ higher design ambition without fee adjustment

The result: effort increases but it becomes harder to see.

The three patterns that cause this

1. Tools are added but workflows are not redesigned

New software is layered onto existing processes rather than replacing them.

2. No one owns the downstream risk

Once a tool affects delivery, risk becomes ambiguous:

-/ Who signs it off?

-/ Who carries liability if it fails?

-/ Who decides when it’s “good enough”?

Without clear ownership, teams default to caution.

3. Time savings convert into invisible complexity

Efficiency rarely results in fewer hours billed.

It results in:

-/ more iterations

-/ more options explored

-/ more information produced

From the outside, productivity looks unchanged but internally, complexity rises.

Why hiring staff often feels “safer” than buying software

Hiring people:

-/ increases visible capacity

-/ spreads risk across individuals

-/ fits existing mental models of delivery

Buying software:

-/ exposes how work is actually done

-/ forces decisions about responsibility

-/ makes inefficiency explicit

This is why practices will hire before they automate - even when automation is cheaper.

A simple sense-check before investing

Before approving any new tool or AI initiative, ask:

-/ What step in our current workflow disappears if this works?

-/ Who is accountable for trusting the output?

-/ What additional checking will we explicitly remove?

-/ Where will the saved time go; fee, quality, or capacity?

If these cannot be answered clearly, the tool will add overhead.

This perspective comes from ongoing work at ADDD with architecture practices assessing how technology decisions impact delivery risk, coordination and cost.

Theme of the Week: AI Rendering & Visualisation Software

Most conversations about AI rendering and visualisation focus on tools. That’s the wrong starting point.

What AI rendering is actually trying to solve is not simply the production of better images. It is addressing long-standing tensions in architectural communication:

-speed vs certainty

-automation vs accountability

-creativity vs consistency

AI dramatically compresses the time between design intent and visual output. That compression is powerful but it also shifts risk. When images can be produced in minutes rather than days, the key question becomes less about capability and more about commitment. What does this image represent, and how will it be interpreted by clients, consultants, and internal teams?

Where practices often struggle is assuming that adopting an AI rendering tool automatically improves communication. In reality, it often accelerates existing issues rather than resolving them.

Three patterns appear consistently.

First, some tools genuinely replace parts of existing processes. They reduce reliance on long rendering pipelines, specialist visualisation bottlenecks, and late-stage image production. Used deliberately, this can free teams to iterate earlier and communicate intent faster.

Second, some tools expose weaknesses in how work is organised. When prompts, reference material, or design assumptions are unclear, outputs become inconsistent. The problem is not the AI; it is the absence of shared understanding about purpose, audience, and stage.

Third, many tools only perform well when upstream information is structured. Clean geometry, clear intent, agreed visual language, and defined approval stages matter more, not less, when AI is introduced.

This is why AI visualisation often creates tension. Client expectations accelerate, while internal certainty has not yet caught up.

AI rendering is not just a production tool. It is a decision-acceleration tool. Practices that recognise this distinction are far more likely to adopt it productively, rather than expensively.

Beyond Titles: Why Capability Will Define Architecture’s Future

Architects achieve extraordinary results despite outdated workflows. That tension sits at the heart of where the profession now stands.

In 2026, my focus is firmly on a future-ready, technology-adept profession. Not in a nostalgic sense. Not by trying to rewind the clock. And not by pretending regulation alone will save us.

Recent commentary from RIBA reinforces something many of us have known for years: in the UK, the title “architect” is protected, but the work is not. Anyone can deliver architectural services, provided they don’t use the name. That isn’t new.

What is new is what comes next.

The real shift facing architects is not about titles or legislation. It is the rapid democratisation of design and delivery tools. AI, automation, and data-driven workflows are already reshaping:

-Who gets to design

-How quickly work is delivered

-How value is defined, priced, and perceived

This creates both an enormous opportunity and an existential threat.

Across my work inside practices, one pattern is consistent: we are behind on AI readiness, behind on workflow maturity, and behind on strategic technology adoption. While the industry debates protection and policy—processes that typically take years—the tools are advancing weekly.

Quality and safety will not be protected by titles alone. They will be protected by capability.

AI, BIM 2.0, rising IT costs, new roles, and new tools are all part of the conversation. But beneath the noise, the real issue is more fundamental. Most practices are not struggling because of technology itself. They are struggling because decisions around technology have been fragmented, reactive, and rarely treated as a core business strategy.

The pieces below reflect that shift. From software costs that are actually IT support problems, to AI acting as a stress test for weak foundations, to where real opportunity is emerging for both ConTech companies and architects themselves.

This is not about chasing trends. It is about understanding what is changing, why it matters, and how to make better decisions going into 2026.

Let’s get into it. 👇.

1. Architects, You Don’t Have a Software Costs Problem, You Have an IT Support Costs Problem.

A quick reflection as the year closes.

This year, the content I shared reached 760,000 impressions and over 143,000 people on LinkedIn. But the numbers matter less than what they revealed. Architects, BIM Managers, and AEC leaders are actively looking for clarity and leadership as AI, BIM 2.0, and new tools reshape practice.

Sharing what I have learned through the Technology Blueprint, and seeing those ideas turn into real conversations, projects, and partnerships, has been the most rewarding part. This ADDDitive newsletter has grown to 2,400+ subscribers, creating space to go deeper into what is actually working inside practices.

Here are my top 5 posts from this year:

Image

The outcome I care about most is simple. Better decisions. Fewer mistakes. A clearer connection between design and technology.

Thank you to everyone who read, challenged, and collaborated this year.
2026 goes deeper, not louder.

2. 760,000 LinkedIn impressions didn’t mean what I thought they did. I assumed Architects were engaging because of AI. They weren’t.

A pattern I did not expect this year.

760,000 LinkedIn impressions initially looked like excitement about AI. It was not. What the engagement really reflected was something more uncomfortable. AI is exposing how weak many technology strategies actually are.

AI is not the problem, and it is not the solution. It is a stress test. When it lands badly in a practice, it usually reveals existing issues. Manual workflows that were never fully fixed. Standards built on habit rather than intent. Tools that do not connect. Decisions made project by project instead of strategically.

Most practices do not need more AI. They need a coherent technology strategy that clarifies what matters now, what can wait, and what should stop altogether.

The response I see is not excitement. It is anxiety, mixed with curiosity. AI touches BIM, IT, data, QA, hardware, software, resourcing, security, and infrastructure. If those foundations are shaky, AI simply makes the cracks visible.

Image

The real question for 2026 is not which AI tool to adopt. It is whether we actually understand how our technology is meant to work together. The firms that win will not be the ones adopting the most tools, but the ones making the fewest bad decisions.

Your product is only as good as the data it’s built on. Outdated, blocked, or missing web sources force your team to fix infrastructure instead of delivering new features.

Teams using Bright Data consistently deliver stable and predictable products, accelerate feature development, and unlock new opportunities with continuous, unblocked web access.

Power Your AI

1. Affinity Is Now Completely Free. And Architects Should Pay Attention

Affinity, the suite that rivals Photoshop, Illustrator, and InDesign, is now 100% free.

No subscriptions.
No “lite” version.
No strings attached.

For years, Adobe has been the default for architectural visuals, reports, and diagrams. But the landscape has been shifting:

  • Rising Creative Cloud subscription fees

  • Limited web-based collaboration

  • Slow development cycles

  • Increasing pressure on practice budgets

And now, after Canva’s acquisition of Serif, Affinity has relaunched as a single all-in-one creative app designed to challenge the monopoly.

This is a genuinely disruptive moment for architects.

Image

What this means for your practice

-Massive cost savings (often thousands per year across a team)

-A single creative environment for reports, presentations, and competition submissions

-Customisable workspaces your teams can standardise and share

-No more vendor lock-in or surprise subscription increases

But more importantly, this signals a broader industry shift:
High-quality, interoperable, affordable software is finally becoming the norm, not the exception. For small studios, independents, and cost-conscious practices, this is game-changing.

I never followed a perfect career plan. I simply followed the problems no one else wanted to solve.

Generate dozens of design possibilities in seconds by adjusting site parameters like form, density, and unit mix, turning iteration into instant insight

Test layouts, iterate with AI, and compare all at once to transform feasibility studies from static reports into live, data-driven simulations.

Unlock your previous collective knowledge by reusing proven layouts, forms, and configurations across new projects.

Set your design parameters and instantly generate multiple options to compare performance, form, and efficiency.

Work together in real time with your team, consultants, and clients on a shared digital model that updates instantly.

Integrate Modern Methods of Construction early to ensure every layout can translate seamlessly into a buildable, modular kit of parts.

Assess daylight, energy, and carbon metrics as you design, aligning creativity with measurable sustainability goals.

8️⃣ Move from Sketch to Data-Driven Insight in One Platform
Sketch, model, and analyse all in the browser, with immediate feedback on performance, cost, and compliance.

Transform early-stage forms into photorealistic visuals within minutes using AI-powered rendering tools.
